# HI5T0RY: Dawn Staley, First USA Basketball Olympic Flag Bearer
**Author**Brooklee Han
**share**Share on TwitterShare on FacebookShare on Email
February 6, 2024
_As part of its 50th Anniversary, USA Basketball is celebrating 50 iconic moments from the organization's history._
Despite a robust collection of Olympic medals, the vast majority being gold, a USA Basketball athlete was not nominated to serve as Olympic Opening Ceremony flag bearer until 2004, exactly 100 years after the spot was first exhibited in an Olympic Games.
The woman tasked with the honor was legendary USA Basketball athlete, and now coach, **Dawn Staley**.
The 2004 Summer Games in Athens, marked Staley’s third trip to the Olympics. A point guard, Staley had helped USA Basketball claim gold in 1996 in Atlanta and 2000 in Sydney. Her Olympic winning streak would continue in Athens, as Staley and the USA beat out Australia 74-63 to clinch gold in the women’s final.

Born and raised in Philadelphia, Staley is the youngest of five children. Staley’s talent on the court was evident from a young age, as she was named the national high school player of the year during her final high school season. She went on to play for four seasons at the University of Virginia before traveling to Europe to play professionally for two seasons. In 1996 she made her U.S. professional basketball debut when she was drafted to play for the American Basketball League’s Richmond Rage. Staley played with the Richmond Rage until 1999, when she moved over to the WNBA, playing for the Charlotte Sting. She remained at part of the Charlotte Sting for eight seasons before retiring from the sport.

# HI5T0RY: Dawn Staley, First USA Basketball Olympic Flag Bearer
During her time in the WNBA Staley began coaching at Temple University during her off seasons, before being hired by the University of South Carolina in 2008 as the head coach of the Gamecocks. Under Staley’s guidance, the South Carolina Gamecocks have captured five SEC regular season championships and two NCAA titles.

Staley’s career as a USA Basketball coach began in 2006, when she we brought in as an assistant coach for the World Championship team. She would go on to serve as an assistant coach for the 2008 and 2016 U.S. Olympic teams. In 2017, Staley was named the head coach of the USA Basketball’s Women’s team through the 2020 Olympics. In Tokyo, Staley became the first Black woman to coach an Olympic team to gold, while her athlete and former teammate Sue Bird became just the second USA Basketball athlete to serve as flag bearer.
Following her USA Basketball coaching career, Staley continues to serve as a member of the USA Women’s National Team Committee.

Title: Kirsty Coventry
Chunks: 6,7,8,9
At the 2005 World Championships in Montreal, Canada, Coventry improved on her 2004 Olympic medal count by winning gold in both the 100 m and 200 m backstroke and silver in the 200 m and the 400 m IM. She bettered her Olympic gold-winning 200 m backstroke time with a performance of 2:08.52. She was one of just two swimmers from Zimbabwe along with Warren Paynter.[28]
In Melbourne, Australia, at the 2007 World Championships, Coventry won silver medals in the 200 m backstroke and 200 m IM. She was disqualified in the 400 m IM when finishing second to eventual winner Katie Hoff in her heat. Coventry finished in a disappointing 14th place in the 100 m backstroke in a time of 1:01.73, failing to qualify for the final. She continued her good form of 2007 by winning four gold medals at the International Swim Meet in Narashino, Japan. She led the way in the 200 m and 400 m IM as well as the 100 m and 200 m backstroke.[29] In the 2007 All-Africa Games in Algiers, Algeria, Coventry won seven gold and three silver medals.[30]
2008 and 2009 seasonsedit  
Coventry in 2009
In 2008, Coventry broke her first world record in the 200 m backstroke at the Missouri Grand Prix. She bettered the mark set by Krisztina Egerszegi in August 1991, the second-oldest swimming world record. Her new record was 2:06.39. Coventry continued her winning streak at the meet by winning the 100 m backstroke and the 200 m IM. Coventry is the third woman in history to break the 1:00 minute barrier in the 100 m backstroke, and the second to break the 59-second barrier.[31]

At the 2008 Manchester Short Course World Championships, Coventry broke her second world record, setting a time, whilst winning the gold medal, of 4:26.52 in the 400 m IM. The following day saw Coventry win her second gold medal of the championships in the 100 m backstroke. Her time of 57:10 was a new championship record and the second-fastest time in history in the event. Only Natalie Coughlin has swum faster (56:51). Day three of the championships saw Coventry break another championship record in qualifying fastest for the final of the 200 m backstroke. Her time of 2:03.69 was a mere four-tenths of a second outside the current world record set by Reiko Nakamura in Tokyo in 2008. Coventry then bettered this time to take her second world record of the championships by winning the final in a time of 2:00.91. She then went on to shatter the short course World Record in winning the 200 m individual medley in 2:06.13.[32]

Coventry represented Zimbabwe at the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, China.[33] Coventry won the silver medal in the 400 metre individual medley event on 10 August 2008, becoming the second woman to swim the medley in less than 4:30, the first being Stephanie Rice who won the gold in the same event. Coventry beat the world record by just under two seconds and was only just beaten by Rice to a new world record. Coventry, in the second semi-final of the 100 m backstroke event, set a new world record of 58.77 seconds. In the final of that event, she was beaten to the gold medal by Natalie Coughlin. Coventry was again beaten by Stephanie Rice in the 200 m individual medley, despite swimming under the former world record. Coventry did defend her Olympic title in the 200 m backstroke, winning gold in a world record time of 2:05.24. She was the country's flag bearer at the closing ceremony. She was the lone member of the delegation to medal, helping win Zimbabwe's most medals at the Olympics ever.[34][35]
Awarded US$100,000 by President Mugabe for her success at the Olympics, Coventry gave that money to charity.[36] At the 2009 World Aquatics Championships in Rome, Italy, Coventry won a gold and a silver. She won the 200 m backstroke world title with a world record time and came second in the 400 m individual medley. She came fourth in the 200 m individual medley final and eighth in the 100 m backstroke final.[37]
2012 and 2016 Olympicsedit

Coventry qualified for her fourth Olympic Games in the 2012 Olympics in London, England. For the first time since 2000, Coventry did not win a medal. She finished third in her semifinal heat of the 200 m individual medley, just edging her into the final, where she placed 6th with a time of 2:11.13. In the 200 m backstroke, she finished outside medal contention in sixth place with a time of 2:08.18. She was given the honor of carrying the Zimbabwean flag into the opening ceremony for the first time.[38] Previously, Coventry won four gold and four silver medals in the 2011 All-Africa Games in Maputo, Mozambique.[39]
Her fifth and final Olympic appearance came at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil,[40] where she repeated her 6th-place performance in the 200 metre backstroke from 2012, with a time of 2:08.80. She also finished 11th in the 100 metre backstroke. She retired after the 2016 Olympics, where she carried the Zimbabwean flag into the stadium during the opening ceremony for the second and final time.[41][42] In her final African Games in 2015, in Brazzaville, the Republic of the Congo, Coventry won three golds and one bronze medals.[43]
Zimbabwean cabinetedit
On 7 September 2018, Coventry was appointed Minister of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation in Zimbabwe's cabinet under Zimbabwean president Emmerson Mnangagwa.[44] Her cabinet role led to her being dubbed "the soft face of Zimbabwe’s dictatorship" as she played a key role in the authoritarian regime.[10][9]

# Former ‘Lost Boy of Sudan’ to Carry U.S. Flag
By Juliet Macur August 6, 2008 10:32 am August 6, 2008 10:32 am
Lopez Lomong was chosen as flag bearer in a vote on Wednesday. (Jonathan Ferrey/Getty Images)
BEIJING – Lopez Lomong, a former child prisoner in war-torn East Africa who was among the so-called Lost Boys of Sudan, will lead the United States Olympic team into a packed National Stadium on Friday night during the opening ceremony of the Olympics.
Just 13 months after becoming a U.S. citizen, Lomong was chosen as flag bearer in a vote on Wednesday. Captains of all the U.S. Olympic teams nominated a flag bearer, from their own sport or another, then cast their ballot.
Lomong, 23, won out, receiving perhaps the most honored position on the U.S. team: He will lead the contingent as it marches into the National Stadium, in the biggest and most anticipated Olympic Games in history.
Lured by the beauty of the democratic process, Lomong had been lobbying for the flag bearer’s position all week at the U.S. track and field training camp in Dalian, China.
“In America, everyone has a chance to do all these things,” Lomong said, according to the Associated Press. “You follow the rules, people will choose, and if I’m blessed to get that opportunity, I’ll get it.”
Lomong’s journey to Olympic competitor in the 1,500-meter race has been harrowing. He was born in Sudan, then was kidnapped and separated from his parents during a civil war. As a prisoner, he watched other boys die of dysentery and starvation.
Eventually, he escaped and made it to a refugee camp in Kenya, where his meals consisted of corn provided by the United Nations.
He spent more than a decade there before coming to the United States in 2001.
As flagbearer for the U.S. team, Lomong follows basketball star Dawn Staley, who held that role in 2004, and kayaker Cliff Meidl, who led the delegation into the Olympic stadium in 2000.

# Former ‘Lost Boy of Sudan’ to Carry U.S. Flag
By Juliet Macur August 6, 2008 10:32 am August 6, 2008 10:32 am
Lopez Lomong was chosen as flag bearer in a vote on Wednesday. (Jonathan Ferrey/Getty Images)
BEIJING – Lopez Lomong, a former child prisoner in war-torn East Africa who was among the so-called Lost Boys of Sudan, will lead the United States Olympic team into a packed National Stadium on Friday night during the opening ceremony of the Olympics.
Just 13 months after becoming a U.S. citizen, Lomong was chosen as flag bearer in a vote on Wednesday. Captains of all the U.S. Olympic teams nominated a flag bearer, from their own sport or another, then cast their ballot.
Lomong, 23, won out, receiving perhaps the most honored position on the U.S. team: He will lead the contingent as it marches into the National Stadium, in the biggest and most anticipated Olympic Games in history.
Lured by the beauty of the democratic process, Lomong had been lobbying for the flag bearer’s position all week at the U.S. track and field training camp in Dalian, China.
“In America, everyone has a chance to do all these things,” Lomong said, according to the Associated Press. “You follow the rules, people will choose, and if I’m blessed to get that opportunity, I’ll get it.”
Lomong’s journey to Olympic competitor in the 1,500-meter race has been harrowing. He was born in Sudan, then was kidnapped and separated from his parents during a civil war. As a prisoner, he watched other boys die of dysentery and starvation.
Eventually, he escaped and made it to a refugee camp in Kenya, where his meals consisted of corn provided by the United Nations.
He spent more than a decade there before coming to the United States in 2001.
As flagbearer for the U.S. team, Lomong follows basketball star Dawn Staley, who held that role in 2004, and kayaker Cliff Meidl, who led the delegation into the Olympic stadium in 2000.

# Former ‘Lost Boy of Sudan’ to Carry U.S. Flag
While I would have preferred if others had been lobbying for Lopez Lomong, I still his selection is an inspired move. First, it shows a touching embrace of a naturalized American, and in the face of some who groused about U.S. Olympic spots going to “foreigners.” Second, of course, is that that is a great way to bring up Darfur, given that virtually every television commentator (except the Chinese and a few of their friends) will surely bring up Sudan, Darfur and China. Yes, it’s a bit political, but China’s whole Olympic hosting is political. I’m very proud of our Olympic team members.

Mr. Lomong, your feet have taken you far……

At the 2005 World Championships in Montreal, Canada, Coventry improved on her 2004 Olympic medal count by winning gold in both the 100 m and 200 m backstroke and silver in the 200 m and the 400 m IM. She bettered her Olympic gold-winning 200 m backstroke time with a performance of 2:08.52. She was one of just two swimmers from Zimbabwe along with Warren Paynter.[28]
In Melbourne, Australia, at the 2007 World Championships, Coventry won silver medals in the 200 m backstroke and 200 m IM. She was disqualified in the 400 m IM when finishing second to eventual winner Katie Hoff in her heat. Coventry finished in a disappointing 14th place in the 100 m backstroke in a time of 1:01.73, failing to qualify for the final. She continued her good form of 2007 by winning four gold medals at the International Swim Meet in Narashino, Japan. She led the way in the 200 m and 400 m IM as well as the 100 m and 200 m backstroke.[29] In the 2007 All-Africa Games in Algiers, Algeria, Coventry won seven gold and three silver medals.[30]
2008 and 2009 seasonsedit  
Coventry in 2009
In 2008, Coventry broke her first world record in the 200 m backstroke at the Missouri Grand Prix. She bettered the mark set by Krisztina Egerszegi in August 1991, the second-oldest swimming world record. Her new record was 2:06.39. Coventry continued her winning streak at the meet by winning the 100 m backstroke and the 200 m IM. Coventry is the third woman in history to break the 1:00 minute barrier in the 100 m backstroke, and the second to break the 59-second barrier.[31]
texts.7: At the 2008 Manchester Short Course World Championships, Coventry broke her second world record, setting a time, whilst winning the gold medal, of 4:26.52 in the 400 m IM. The following day saw Coventry win her second gold medal of the championships in the 100 m backstroke. Her time of 57:10 was a new championship record and the second-fastest time in history in the event. Only Natalie Coughlin has swum faster (56:51). Day three of the championships saw Coventry break another championship record in qualifying fastest for the final of the 200 m backstroke. Her time of 2:03.69 was a mere four-tenths of a second outside the current world record set by Reiko Nakamura in Tokyo in 2008. Coventry then bettered this time to take her second world record of the championships by winning the final in a time of 2:00.91. She then went on to shatter the short course World Record in winning the 200 m individual medley in 2:06.13.[32]
texts.8:
Coventry represented Zimbabwe at the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, China.[33] Coventry won the silver medal in the 400 metre individual medley event on 10 August 2008, becoming the second woman to swim the medley in less than 4:30, the first being Stephanie Rice who won the gold in the same event. Coventry beat the world record by just under two seconds and was only just beaten by Rice to a new world record. Coventry, in the second semi-final of the 100 m backstroke event, set a new world record of 58.77 seconds. In the final of that event, she was beaten to the gold medal by Natalie Coughlin. Coventry was again beaten by Stephanie Rice in the 200 m individual medley, despite swimming under the former world record. Coventry did defend her Olympic title in the 200 m backstroke, winning gold in a world record time of 2:05.24. She was the country's flag bearer at the closing ceremony. She was the lone member of the delegation to medal, helping win Zimbabwe's most medals at the Olympics ever.[34][35]
Awarded US$100,000 by President Mugabe for her success at the Olympics, Coventry gave that money to charity.[36] At the 2009 World Aquatics Championships in Rome, Italy, Coventry won a gold and a silver. She won the 200 m backstroke world title with a world record time and came second in the 400 m individual medley. She came fourth in the 200 m individual medley final and eighth in the 100 m backstroke final.[37]
2012 and 2016 Olympicsedit
texts.9:
Coventry qualified for her fourth Olympic Games in the 2012 Olympics in London, England. For the first time since 2000, Coventry did not win a medal. She finished third in her semifinal heat of the 200 m individual medley, just edging her into the final, where she placed 6th with a time of 2:11.13. In the 200 m backstroke, she finished outside medal contention in sixth place with a time of 2:08.18. She was given the honor of carrying the Zimbabwean flag into the opening ceremony for the first time.[38] Previously, Coventry won four gold and four silver medals in the 2011 All-Africa Games in Maputo, Mozambique.[39]
Her fifth and final Olympic appearance came at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil,[40] where she repeated her 6th-place performance in the 200 metre backstroke from 2012, with a time of 2:08.80. She also finished 11th in the 100 metre backstroke. She retired after the 2016 Olympics, where she carried the Zimbabwean flag into the stadium during the opening ceremony for the second and final time.[41][42] In her final African Games in 2015, in Brazzaville, the Republic of the Congo, Coventry won three golds and one bronze medals.[43]
Zimbabwean cabinetedit
On 7 September 2018, Coventry was appointed Minister of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation in Zimbabwe's cabinet under Zimbabwean president Emmerson Mnangagwa.[44] Her cabinet role led to her being dubbed "the soft face of Zimbabwe’s dictatorship" as she played a key role in the authoritarian regime.[10][9]

The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines
by TOWN & COUNTRY PHILIPPINES | NOV 9, 2016
BELMONTE
This powerful and inspiring family influences countless Filipinos daily through its newspaper business as well as through politics. Though Betty Go Belmonte passed away more than 20 years ago, her legacy is still felt through the Philippine Star, a newspaper she co-founded in 1986. The daughter of Go Puan Seng of the Fookien Times, Betty married Feliciano Belmonte, a lawyer and former reporter for the Manila Chronicle (and now Speaker of the House of Representatives)—so publishing and politics clearly runs in the family’s veins. The couple’s children have followed their lead: Miguel, Kevin, and Isaac Belmonte split duties at the Philippine Star, while daughter Joy is the vice mayor of Quezon City.
BENITEZ

# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
For many years, the extended Benitez family has produced writers, politicians, and educators. Among the most celebrated is 99-year-old Helena Benitez, the daughter of Philippine Women’s University founders Conrado Benitez and Francisca Tirona. Tita Helen, as she is fondly called, has been a senator, diplomat, arts and culture patron (she helped found the Bayanihan dance troupe) and women’s rights advocate. The Benitez family compound, Mira Nila in San Juan, has been declared a National Heritage Site, while the university is currently being run by a fourth generation member, Francisco B. Benitez.
PRIETO
The Philippine Daily Inquirer’s chair, Marixi Prieto, is also a scion of another family on this list, the Rufinos. Two of Marixi’s five children with husband Alex work with the daily: Sandy P. Romualdez is the president and CEO, while Tessa has a lifestyle column. Another prominent branch of the Prieto family stems from Leo’s cousin, the late Leo Prieto, a sportsman and founding commissioner of the Philippine Basketball Association. Married to society doyenne and queen of etiquette, Mary Prieto, Leo’s children include Marylou Lovina, Leo Jr., and Mike Prieto.
RAMOS
The slogan of National Book Store’s loyalty card rings true: so many of us love books because we are “laking National.” The founder of the ubiquitous chain of stores has just turned 90, but Nanay Coring shows no signs of slowing down. Despite her success, she still prays for the same things every night. “Good health, good business, and please help me pay the utang,” she revealed to the Philippine Daily Inquirer. Among her children, Alfredo runs Atlas Mining, Ben is an entrepreneur (Virgie Ramos of Gift Gate is his wife), and Cecilia is National’s vice president for purchasing.
ROBREDO

# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
Though taken from us far too soon, the late Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jesse Robredo continues to inspire thanks to his honesty, integrity, and dedication to serve. His efforts did not go unrecognized during his lifetime, thankfully, as he was honored with the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2000 for his public service. With her husband as a guiding light, his widow Leni has picked up the fight against traditional politics, successfully becoming Vice President of the Philippines after a term in Congress.
AQUINO
When Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III ran for president in 2010, he had a number of things going for him, but perhaps the most important was the legacy of the Aquino name. His father Ninoy was widely admired for his uncompromising stand against the Marcos administration—his assassination in 1983 sparked a chain of events that ultimately led to Marcos’ ouster three years later—while his mother Cory was a symbol of virtue and honesty during her six-year term as president.

The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines
by TOWN & COUNTRY PHILIPPINES | NOV 9, 2016
BELMONTE
This powerful and inspiring family influences countless Filipinos daily through its newspaper business as well as through politics. Though Betty Go Belmonte passed away more than 20 years ago, her legacy is still felt through the Philippine Star, a newspaper she co-founded in 1986. The daughter of Go Puan Seng of the Fookien Times, Betty married Feliciano Belmonte, a lawyer and former reporter for the Manila Chronicle (and now Speaker of the House of Representatives)—so publishing and politics clearly runs in the family’s veins. The couple’s children have followed their lead: Miguel, Kevin, and Isaac Belmonte split duties at the Philippine Star, while daughter Joy is the vice mayor of Quezon City.
BENITEZ
texts.2:
# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
For many years, the extended Benitez family has produced writers, politicians, and educators. Among the most celebrated is 99-year-old Helena Benitez, the daughter of Philippine Women’s University founders Conrado Benitez and Francisca Tirona. Tita Helen, as she is fondly called, has been a senator, diplomat, arts and culture patron (she helped found the Bayanihan dance troupe) and women’s rights advocate. The Benitez family compound, Mira Nila in San Juan, has been declared a National Heritage Site, while the university is currently being run by a fourth generation member, Francisco B. Benitez.
PRIETO
The Philippine Daily Inquirer’s chair, Marixi Prieto, is also a scion of another family on this list, the Rufinos. Two of Marixi’s five children with husband Alex work with the daily: Sandy P. Romualdez is the president and CEO, while Tessa has a lifestyle column. Another prominent branch of the Prieto family stems from Leo’s cousin, the late Leo Prieto, a sportsman and founding commissioner of the Philippine Basketball Association. Married to society doyenne and queen of etiquette, Mary Prieto, Leo’s children include Marylou Lovina, Leo Jr., and Mike Prieto.
RAMOS
The slogan of National Book Store’s loyalty card rings true: so many of us love books because we are “laking National.” The founder of the ubiquitous chain of stores has just turned 90, but Nanay Coring shows no signs of slowing down. Despite her success, she still prays for the same things every night. “Good health, good business, and please help me pay the utang,” she revealed to the Philippine Daily Inquirer. Among her children, Alfredo runs Atlas Mining, Ben is an entrepreneur (Virgie Ramos of Gift Gate is his wife), and Cecilia is National’s vice president for purchasing.
ROBREDO
texts.3:
# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
Though taken from us far too soon, the late Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jesse Robredo continues to inspire thanks to his honesty, integrity, and dedication to serve. His efforts did not go unrecognized during his lifetime, thankfully, as he was honored with the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2000 for his public service. With her husband as a guiding light, his widow Leni has picked up the fight against traditional politics, successfully becoming Vice President of the Philippines after a term in Congress.
AQUINO
When Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III ran for president in 2010, he had a number of things going for him, but perhaps the most important was the legacy of the Aquino name. His father Ninoy was widely admired for his uncompromising stand against the Marcos administration—his assassination in 1983 sparked a chain of events that ultimately led to Marcos’ ouster three years later—while his mother Cory was a symbol of virtue and honesty during her six-year term as president.

The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines
by TOWN & COUNTRY PHILIPPINES | NOV 9, 2016
BELMONTE
This powerful and inspiring family influences countless Filipinos daily through its newspaper business as well as through politics. Though Betty Go Belmonte passed away more than 20 years ago, her legacy is still felt through the Philippine Star, a newspaper she co-founded in 1986. The daughter of Go Puan Seng of the Fookien Times, Betty married Feliciano Belmonte, a lawyer and former reporter for the Manila Chronicle (and now Speaker of the House of Representatives)—so publishing and politics clearly runs in the family’s veins. The couple’s children have followed their lead: Miguel, Kevin, and Isaac Belmonte split duties at the Philippine Star, while daughter Joy is the vice mayor of Quezon City.
BENITEZ
texts.2:
# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
For many years, the extended Benitez family has produced writers, politicians, and educators. Among the most celebrated is 99-year-old Helena Benitez, the daughter of Philippine Women’s University founders Conrado Benitez and Francisca Tirona. Tita Helen, as she is fondly called, has been a senator, diplomat, arts and culture patron (she helped found the Bayanihan dance troupe) and women’s rights advocate. The Benitez family compound, Mira Nila in San Juan, has been declared a National Heritage Site, while the university is currently being run by a fourth generation member, Francisco B. Benitez.
PRIETO
The Philippine Daily Inquirer’s chair, Marixi Prieto, is also a scion of another family on this list, the Rufinos. Two of Marixi’s five children with husband Alex work with the daily: Sandy P. Romualdez is the president and CEO, while Tessa has a lifestyle column. Another prominent branch of the Prieto family stems from Leo’s cousin, the late Leo Prieto, a sportsman and founding commissioner of the Philippine Basketball Association. Married to society doyenne and queen of etiquette, Mary Prieto, Leo’s children include Marylou Lovina, Leo Jr., and Mike Prieto.
RAMOS
The slogan of National Book Store’s loyalty card rings true: so many of us love books because we are “laking National.” The founder of the ubiquitous chain of stores has just turned 90, but Nanay Coring shows no signs of slowing down. Despite her success, she still prays for the same things every night. “Good health, good business, and please help me pay the utang,” she revealed to the Philippine Daily Inquirer. Among her children, Alfredo runs Atlas Mining, Ben is an entrepreneur (Virgie Ramos of Gift Gate is his wife), and Cecilia is National’s vice president for purchasing.
ROBREDO
texts.3:
# Memories of Old Manila & Beyond | The Most Inspiring Families of the Philippines | Facebook
Though taken from us far too soon, the late Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jesse Robredo continues to inspire thanks to his honesty, integrity, and dedication to serve. His efforts did not go unrecognized during his lifetime, thankfully, as he was honored with the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2000 for his public service. With her husband as a guiding light, his widow Leni has picked up the fight against traditional politics, successfully becoming Vice President of the Philippines after a term in Congress.
AQUINO
When Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III ran for president in 2010, he had a number of things going for him, but perhaps the most important was the legacy of the Aquino name. His father Ninoy was widely admired for his uncompromising stand against the Marcos administration—his assassination in 1983 sparked a chain of events that ultimately led to Marcos’ ouster three years later—while his mother Cory was a symbol of virtue and honesty during her six-year term as president.

First Winter Games held in a different year from the Summer Games. Widely considered the best Winter Games, featuring an opening ceremony on a ski jump venue, whose climax was skier Stein Gruben going downhill with the Torch before the Cauldron was lit by Crown Prince Haakon, whose father, King Harald V, and grandfather, Olav V, were themselves Olympians. The Games featured the domination of women's cross-country events by Italy's Manuela Di Centa and Russia's Lyubov Yegorova, with 5 and 4 medals, respectively, a heartstopping victory of Italy over Norway in the men's 4×10km cross-country event by just 0.4 second, and American speed skater Dan Jansen, long considered a favorite but beleaguered by failure ever since 1988, when he had to compete even as he was mourning his older sister Jane, who died of leukemia hours before his first event, finally winning the 1000m event. A tabloid-friendly scandal involving rival American figure skaters Nancy Kerrigan and Tonya Harding provided fodder for comedians and sketch comedy shows for months; Harding never lived it down. A Norwegian-English mockumentary can be seen here, even though it has a "For all ages" rating in Norway is it NSFW.
*   **XVIII — 1998: Nagano, Japan**  
**Motto:** "Coexistence with Nature"
**Duration:** February 7-22
**Participating Athletes:** 2,176 (1,389 men, 787 women) from 72 NOCs note
**Mascots:** The Snowlets (snowy owls)—Sukki, Nokki, Lekki, and Tsukki note
**Olympic Oaths:** Kenji Ogiwara note [Athletes] / Junko Hiramatsu note [Judges]
**Carriers of the Torch and Lighter of the Flame:** Chris Moon note, accompanied by children representing the participating nations / Masako Chiba note / Reiichi Mikata, Takanori Kono and Kenji Ogiwara note / Hiromi Suzuki note / _Midori Ito_ note

## Winter Olympic Games
The first Winter Games featuring women's ice hockey, curling and snowboarding. It was also the first time NHL players were allowed to play in men's ice hockey. The bobsled track used for these games was notable for having a portion that sloped **up**hill. The Games featured 15-year-old American figure skater Tara Lipinski beating compatriot Michelle Kwan to become the youngest individual champion in the history of the Winter Olympics and Austrian skier Hermann Maier, who survived a hard fall days before the Games, winning the Super-G and giant slalom events. These are, to date, the last Winter Olympics - as well as Olympics, period - to be televised in the United States by a network other than NBC (in this case, CBS, in partnership with Turner Sports).
*   **XIX — 2002: Salt Lake City, Utah, United States**note  
**Motto:** "Light the Fire Within"
**Duration:** February 8-24
**Participating Athletes:** 2,399 (1,513 men, 886 women) from 78 NOCs note
**Mascots:** Powder the hare, Copper the coyote, and Coal the black bear (Olympics)note / Otto the otter (Paralympics)note
**Bearers of the Olympic Flag:** John Glenn note (Americas), Desmond Tutu note (Africa), Kazuyoshi Funaki note (Asia), Lech Wałęsa note (Europe), Cathy Freeman (Oceania), Jean-Claude Killy note (Sport), Steven Spielberg (Culture) and Jean-Michel Cousteau note (Environment)

## Winter Olympic Games
Notable for a bribery controversy, the disclosure of which forced several IOC members to resign; the same scandal led to the appointment of a certain Boston-based financier named Mitt Romney to head the Organizing Committee, which he leveraged into his run for Governor of Massachusetts and later the Presidency. The scores of a figure-skating judge were also thrown out, resulting in two couples being awarded gold medals for pairs skating. And American short track speed skater Apolo Ohno's first gold was awarded after South Korea's Kim Dong-sung was disqualified, resulting in over 16,000 threatening emails to the IOC's website, which shut the site down for almost nine hours (it also didn't help that Ohno is half-Japanese). Nevertheless, from a financial and sporting perspective, these Games were one of the most successful. These Games featured Canada's first men's ice hockey gold since 1952, Norwegian biathlete Ole Einar Bjørndalen winning all four men's events, and short track speed skating providing the first gold medals for China, courtesy of Yang Yang (A) in women's competitions, and Australia (and, for that matter, the entire southern hemisphere), courtesy of Steven Bradbury's unlikely come-from-dead-last finish after everybody else crashed out on the final turn Also noteworthy for being the first games (outside of St. Moritz) to feature Skeleton, a sliding sport described as being "Like luge, but face-down and head-first". Also the first ever Olympics to feature Skeleton competing on the same track as bobsled and luge (St. Moritz had a separate skeleton track) US Men's Skeleton athlete Jimmy Shea took gold, being America's first ever third-generation Olympian. The opening ceremonies were notable for their inclusion of the American flag that flew at the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, during the national anthem, in order to honor the victims of the attack which occurred just six months before.

The Games featured Russian figure skater Evgeni Plushenko setting a world record for the largest margin of victory in his event (10 points), Apollo Ohno winning his second short track speed skating event (and this time without much controversy), and Italian cross-country skier Giorgio Di Centa, younger brother of Manuela, winning both the 4×10km and 50km events (the latter which held its medals ceremony at the closing ceremony, in the presence of his sister). The opening ceremony is notable for beginning with 1996 gymnastics gold medalist Yuri Chechi playing the role of a "shaman" striking at a fire-breathing anvil, a live F1 race car demonstration, and the final public performance of legendary tenor Luciano Pavarotti, who performed "Nessun Dorma" at the end of the opening ceremony, less than a year before he died of pancreatic cancer.

## Winter Olympic Games
**Mascots:** Miga the mythical orca/kermode bear hybrid, Quatchi the sasquatch (Olympics), Sumi the thunderbird/bear hybrid (Paralympics), and Mukmuk the Vancouver Island marmot (sidekick)note

The Winter Games that ended Canada's dry spell when it comes to gold medals on Games it hosts, starting with Alexandre Bilodeau in men's moguls, followed by thirteen others, culminating in a heart-stopping overtime victory of the Canadian men's ice hockey team over the USA. This broke the record for most golds at a single games, which had been previously shared by Norway and the Soviet Union. Other notable events include USA winning its first bobsled gold since 1948, American skier Lindsey Vonn shrugging off injury to win gold at the women's downhill, and another American, Evan Lysacek, pipping out Plushenko for the men's figure skating gold. The Games, however, began with tragedy after Georgian luger Nodar Kumaritashvili was killed in a training accident mere hours before the opening ceremony.

**Motto:** "Hot. Cool. Yours."

## Winter Olympic Games
An unusual choice for Winter Olympic host city, being both a winter _and_ summer resort town. Also the first Games under current IOC president, 1976 fencing gold medalist Thomas Bach. While the runoff was fraught with controversy, due to allegations of corruption, outrage over anti-gay laws, and a staggering $51B cost (far surpassing Beijing 2008's $44B, which, as a summer edition, had more events and, all things said, is not terribly over-expensive), the main event itself went without a hitch. The Games featured a near-total domination of speed skating events by the Dutch, the Canadian men's ice hockey team making the first successful gold medal defense since the Soviet Union, promising American skier Mikaela Shiffrin becoming the youngest alpine skiing gold medalist at eighteen years old, childhood friends Meryl Davis and Charlie White winning the USA's first ice dancing gold, and Ole Einar Bjørndalen winning the 10km sprint and mixed relay, setting a record for most decorated Winter Olympian with eight golds, four silvers and one bronze. Years after these Games, host Russia has been mired in a massive scandal over allegations of state-sponsored doping and deliberately tampering with any incriminatory evidence, extending even onto Summer Games sports, resulting in thirteen medals revoked (though nine were ultimately returned after an appeal), the Russian track team for the 2016 Summer Games at Rio de Janeiro being almost entirely banned, and the outright suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in 2017, resulting in athletes who can prove themselves clean having to compete as neutrals come the next Winter Games at Pyeongchang and the 2020 Summer Games in Tokyo.

## The Olympic Torch and Torch Relay
### Torch Route
*   **Kaffrine (12 October):** Located in the center of the country, in the transition zone between the peanut basin and the eastern regions. Celebration site: Stade municipal El Hadji Babacar Gaye.  
*   **Tambacounda (14 October):** Located in eastern Senegal, one of the country’s largest regions and serving as a gateway to the eastern areas. Celebration site: Stade régional de Tambacounda.  
*   **Kédougou (16 October):** Located in the far southeast of Senegal, known for its rugged terrain and proximity to Mali and Guinea. Celebration site: Place Léopold Sédar Senghor.  
*   **Kolda (18 October):** Located in southern Senegal in Upper Casamance, distinguished by its lush landscapes and cultural heritage. Celebration site: Stade municipal de Kolda.  
*   **Sédhiou (19 October):** Located in Casamance in southern Senegal, along the banks of the Casamance River. Celebration site: Stade municipal de Sédhiou.  
*   **Ziguinchor (21–22 October):** The main city of Casamance in southwestern Senegal, serving as a vital urban and cultural center for the region. Celebration site: Stade Aline Sitoé Diatta.  
*   **Saly (24 October):** An important tourism center located on the Petite Côte within the Thiès region and one of the host regions for Dakar 2026.  
*   **Dakar – Final Stage:** 26 October Rufisque; 27 October Pikine; 28 October Guédiawaye; 29 October Gorée; 30 October Dakar, Place de la Nation. This final stage will take place on the eve of the Games’ opening ceremony and will mark the culmination of weeks of journeying.
On 31 October, the torch will take center stage at the Opening Ceremony in Dakar, symbolizing the energy shared across the nation.

## The Olympic Torch and Torch Relay
### Torchbearers
Torchbearers have been selected locally in each region. Athletes, public figures, young talents, civil society representatives, and prominent individuals from the regions will participate in the relay. The following individuals are among the torchbearers:
*   **Amadou Dia Bâ (Athletics):** Born in Dakar in 1958; competed in the 1984, 1988 and 1992 Olympic Games; won a silver medal in the 400 metres hurdles at the 1988 Seoul Olympics with a time of 47.23 seconds, a record that still stands as the Senegalese national record. He has won five African championships, claimed victory at the 1987 African Games, and is Senegal’s only Olympic medalist in history.  
*   **Isabelle Sambou (Wrestling):** One of the leading figures in women’s wrestling in Senegal, she has won multiple African championships and competed at the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Olympic Games. As a coach, she encourages young girls to participate in sports.  
*   **Malick Fall (Swimming):** Specialist in breaststroke; competed in four Olympic Games from Sydney 2000 to London 2012 and was Senegal’s flag bearer at the 2004 Athens Olympics. He has won numerous medals at African Championships and African Games. After a career spanning more than twenty years at the highest level, he now works as a coach and mentor to young swimmers.  
*   **Dame Ndao (Karate):** Holder of a 6th dan black belt; twelve-time Senegalese champion, three-time African champion and two-time participant in the World Championships. The teams he coached between 2010 and 2014 won 62 medals in the senior category. He is a former president of the National Technical Commission.  
*   **Aïcha Adama Fal (Kung Fu Wushu):** Born in Louga; five-time Senegalese champion between 2021 and 2025 and ten-time champion of regional club competitions. She won a silver medal at the 2026 African Kung Fu Wushu Championship held in Cairo.  

## The Olympic Torch and Torch Relay
### Torchbearers
*   **Khaby Lame (Content Creator):** Italian-Senegalese content creator born in Mbacké; followed by hundreds of millions worldwide and the most followed content creator on TikTok. On 26 March 2026, he was officially appointed as the Dakar 2026 ambassador; he will participate in the Torch Relay and in inclusion initiatives targeting youth in his hometown.  
*   **Amadou Gallo Fall (Sports Administrator):** President of the Basketball Africa League (BAL) and former vice president and general manager of NBA Africa. He founded the SEED association (Sports for Education and Economic Development) in 1998 and received the Naismith Legacy Award in 2023.  
*   **Adama Diallo (Civil Society):** Works in the field of women’s leadership and civil participation in Casamance. Since 2022, she has coordinated the “Young Girls Leadership Clubs” in Kolda; appointed as UNICEF Senegal Youth Advocate in 2022 and recipient of the Casamance Leadership Award in 2024.  
*   **Omar Sy (Actor):** French-Senegalese actor of Senegalese and Mauritanian origin (_Intouchables_, _Lupin_, _Jurassic World_) and official Dakar 2026 ambassador.

## Participant Programs
*   **Athlete Role Models:** Will provide on-site mentoring and workshop training for young athletes during Dakar 2026.  
*   **IOC Young Reporters Programme:** A programme organized and managed by IOC Media Operations, aimed at developing the next generation of sports journalists; promotes international cooperation, cultural exchange and Olympic values.  
*   **Athlete365:** A dedicated webpage has been created for athletes competing at the Youth Olympic Games to develop new skills outside of sport.

## Promotional Activities
Dakar 2026 has planned various activities to engage fans during the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. The Île-Saint-Denis area has been transformed into "Africa Station," a fan zone dedicated to African culture and sport, and Dakar 2026 participated in these celebrations with a special event program throughout the Games. Additionally, live broadcast areas with large screens interactive workshops artistic events and sports activities were organized at Parc Georges-Valbon in Seine-Saint-Denis.

## Türkiye's Participation
### Participation in Dakar 2026
Türkiye will compete in Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games with 34 athletes (14 women and 20 men) across 16 disciplines. The participation was announced by the Turkish National Olympic Committee (TNOC). The TNOC lists 3x3 Basketball Athletics Baseball/Softball Cycling Breaking Football Futsal Skateboarding Table Tennis Beach Wrestling Beach Volleyball Taekwondo Wushu and Swimming as the disciplines for Dakar 2026.

## Türkiye's Participation
### Participation in Previous Games
Türkiye has participated in the Youth Olympic Games in Singapore 2010 Nanjing 2014 and Buenos Aires 2018 winning a total of 34 medals.
*   **Singapore 2010:** 55 athletes comprising 29 women and 26 men. Total of 13 medals: 2 in boxing 1 in gymnastics 1 in fencing 1 in football 3 in wrestling 1 in weightlifting 1 in judo 1 in archery and 2 in taekwondo.  
*   **Nanjing 2014:** 42 athletes comprising 21 women and 21 men. Total of 10 medals: 2 in boxing 3 in wrestling 2 in judo 2 in taekwondo and 1 in shot put.  
*   **Buenos Aires 2018:** 56 athletes comprising 30 women and 26 men. Total of 11 medals: 4 in weightlifting 3 in athletics 2 in wrestling 1 in judo and 1 in karate.

These Games featured Canada's first men's ice hockey gold since 1952, Norwegian biathlete Ole Einar Bjørndalen winning all four men's events, and short track speed skating providing the first gold medals for China, courtesy of Yang Yang (A) in women's competitions, and Australia (and, for that matter, the entire southern hemisphere), courtesy of Steven Bradbury's unlikely come-from-dead-last finish after everybody else crashed out on the final turn Also noteworthy for being the first games (outside of St. Moritz) to feature Skeleton, a sliding sport described as being "Like luge, but face-down and head-first". Also the first ever Olympics to feature Skeleton competing on the same track as bobsled and luge (St. Moritz had a separate skeleton track) US Men's Skeleton athlete Jimmy Shea took gold, being America's first ever third-generation Olympian. The opening ceremonies were notable for their inclusion of the American flag that flew at the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001, during the national anthem, in order to honor the victims of the attack which occurred just six months before.
*   **XX — 2006: Turin (aka "Torino"), Piedmont, Italy**  
**Motto:** "Passion Lives Here"
**Duration:** February 10-26
**Participating Athletes:** 2,508 (1,548 men, 960 women) from 80 NOCs note

## Winter Olympic Games
**Mascots:** Neve the snowball and Gliz the ice cube (Olympics)note / Aster the snowflake (Paralympics)note
**Bearers of the Olympic Flag:**Sophia Lorennote, Isabel Allendenote, Nawal el Moutawakel note, Susan Sarandon note, Wangari Maathai note, Manuela Di Centa note, Maria Mutola note and Somaly Mam note
**Olympic Oaths:** Giorgio Rocca note [Athletes] / Fabio Bianchetti note [Judges]
**Carriers of the Torch and Lighter of the Flame:** Alberto Tomba note / Marco Albarello, Giorgio Vanzetta, Maurilio De Zolt and Silvio Fauner note / Piero Gros note / Deborah Compagnoni note / _Stefania Belmondo_ note
The Games featured Russian figure skater Evgeni Plushenko setting a world record for the largest margin of victory in his event (10 points), Apollo Ohno winning his second short track speed skating event (and this time without much controversy), and Italian cross-country skier Giorgio Di Centa, younger brother of Manuela, winning both the 4×10km and 50km events (the latter which held its medals ceremony at the closing ceremony, in the presence of his sister). The opening ceremony is notable for beginning with 1996 gymnastics gold medalist Yuri Chechi playing the role of a "shaman" striking at a fire-breathing anvil, a live F1 race car demonstration, and the final public performance of legendary tenor Luciano Pavarotti, who performed "Nessun Dorma" at the end of the opening ceremony, less than a year before he died of pancreatic cancer.
*   **XXI — 2010: Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada**  
**Motto:** "With Glowing Hearts / Des plus brillants exploits"note
**Duration:** February 12-28
**Participating Athletes:** 2,566 (1,522 men, 1,044 women) from 82 NOCs note

## Winter Olympic Games
**Mascots:** Miga the mythical orca/kermode bear hybrid, Quatchi the sasquatch (Olympics), Sumi the thunderbird/bear hybrid (Paralympics), and Mukmuk the Vancouver Island marmot (sidekick)note
**Bearers of the Olympic Flag:** Betty Fox note, Donald Sutherlandnote, Jacques Villeneuve note, Barbara Ann Scott note, Anne Murray note, Roméo Dallaire note, Bobby Orr note and Julie Payette note
**Olympic Oaths:** Hayley Wickenheiser note [Athletes] / Michel Verrault note [Judges]
**Carrier of the Torch and Lighters of the Flame:** Rick Hansen / _Catriona LeMay Doan_ note _, Steve Nash_ note _, Nancy Greene_ note _and Wayne Gretzky_ note Added note
The Winter Games that ended Canada's dry spell when it comes to gold medals on Games it hosts, starting with Alexandre Bilodeau in men's moguls, followed by thirteen others, culminating in a heart-stopping overtime victory of the Canadian men's ice hockey team over the USA. This broke the record for most golds at a single games, which had been previously shared by Norway and the Soviet Union. Other notable events include USA winning its first bobsled gold since 1948, American skier Lindsey Vonn shrugging off injury to win gold at the women's downhill, and another American, Evan Lysacek, pipping out Plushenko for the men's figure skating gold. The Games, however, began with tragedy after Georgian luger Nodar Kumaritashvili was killed in a training accident mere hours before the opening ceremony.

**Motto:** "Hot. Cool. Yours."

texts.64:
## Winter Olympic Games
An unusual choice for Winter Olympic host city, being both a winter _and_ summer resort town. Also the first Games under current IOC president, 1976 fencing gold medalist Thomas Bach. While the runoff was fraught with controversy, due to allegations of corruption, outrage over anti-gay laws, and a staggering $51B cost (far surpassing Beijing 2008's $44B, which, as a summer edition, had more events and, all things said, is not terribly over-expensive), the main event itself went without a hitch. The Games featured a near-total domination of speed skating events by the Dutch, the Canadian men's ice hockey team making the first successful gold medal defense since the Soviet Union, promising American skier Mikaela Shiffrin becoming the youngest alpine skiing gold medalist at eighteen years old, childhood friends Meryl Davis and Charlie White winning the USA's first ice dancing gold, and Ole Einar Bjørndalen winning the 10km sprint and mixed relay, setting a record for most decorated Winter Olympian with eight golds, four silvers and one bronze. Years after these Games, host Russia has been mired in a massive scandal over allegations of state-sponsored doping and deliberately tampering with any incriminatory evidence, extending even onto Summer Games sports, resulting in thirteen medals revoked (though nine were ultimately returned after an appeal), the Russian track team for the 2016 Summer Games at Rio de Janeiro being almost entirely banned, and the outright suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in 2017, resulting in athletes who can prove themselves clean having to compete as neutrals come the next Winter Games at Pyeongchang and the 2020 Summer Games in Tokyo.
*   **XXIII — 2018: PyeongChang, South Korea**  
**Motto:** "Passion. Connected."
**Duration:** February 9-25
**Participating Athletes:** 2,922 (1,680 men, 1,242 women) from 94 NOCs note
**Mascots:** Soohorang the white tiger (Olympics) and Bandabi the black bear (Paralympics)note

The 2004 Summer Games in Athens, marked Staley’s third trip to the Olympics. A point guard, Staley had helped USA Basketball claim gold in 1996 in Atlanta and 2000 in Sydney. Her Olympic winning streak would continue in Athens, as Staley and the USA beat out Australia 74-63 to clinch gold in the women’s final.

Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and current President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC). She won Olympic gold medals in the 2004 and 2008 Summer Games in women's swimming. She is an NCAA champion swimmer. She is currently presiding over the XXV Winter Olympic Games, the first games under her leadership. She is 42 years old (September 16, 1983) and was born in Harare, Zimbabwe, the country's capital and largest city.
Coventry was taught to swim by her mother when he was just a toddler in the family pool. She was inspired to compete at the Olympic level when she was watching the 1992 Games in Barcelona on television. She was a multi-sport athlete as a kid, competing in tennis, field hockey, and cross-country running. She focused on swimming after a knee injury as a young teen.

# Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and... - Living Legend Bios | Facebook
## Living Legend Bios's Post
Coventry competed in four events in the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, representing Zimbabwe. Her best finish was 12th in the 100m backstroke. After the Olympics, she moved to the United States and attended Auburn University on a scholarship. The Tigers dominated in swimming in the early 21st century with stars like Margaret Hoelzer, Eileen Coparropa, Maggie Bowen, and Coventry. The Tigers won three consecutive team NCAA championships (2002-04) while she was there under coach David Marsh. They were runner-up during her senior year in 2005. She won seven individual titles in her four years at Auburn. She earned a degree in Hotel and Restaurant Management.
In the middle of her collegiate career, Coventry made a return visit to the Olympics, this time to the 2004 Games in Athens. She won three medals, including a gold in the 200m backstroke. They were the only medals won by athletes from Zimbabwe. She wasn't done. She shattered the old world record by nearly a full second to defend her gold medal in the 2008 Games in Beijing. She set a world record in the semifinals of the 100m backstroke but was edged out for the gold by American Natalie Coughlin in the finals by about a quarter second. Coventry won two other silver medals at the games. She served as flag bearer for Zimbabwe in the closing ceremony.
Coventry returned to the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Games in London. This time, she was the flag bearer for the African country in the opening ceremony. She was hampered by pneumonia and injuring and her best finish was sixth. She was 32 years old when she last competed in the 2016 Summer Games in Rio de Janeiro, where she once again carried the Zimbabwean flag. Again, her best finish was sixth. She retired from competitive swimming after the 2016 Games.

In 2012, Coventry was elected to the IOC Athletes' Commission. As a representative of that commission, she was elected as an IOC Member in 2013. She started on the IOC Executive Board in 2018. She was also appointed Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture in her home country by Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa in 2018. In 2025, she was elected as the 10th President of the IOC, succeeding German Thomas Bach, who served for nearly 12 years. On Friday (February 6th), she delivered a riveting speech in Milan, Italy, when the XXV Winter Olympic Games were declared open. The Games are expected to conclude on February 22. Her initial term ends in 2033.
Coventry and her husband founded The Kirsty Coventry Academy in 2015 to help address the high rate of drowning in her home country. It helps teach children from disadvantaged backgrounds swimming skills. They launched a program called HEROES (Health, Education, Recreation, Opportunity, Empowerment, Sport) in 2017 and provides free access to multi-sports for the children of Zimbabwe.
Coventry (pictured left in 2026) has two daughters (Ella pictured right in 2019) with Tyrone Seward. They have been married for 12 years. They primarily live in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Following her USA Basketball coaching career, Staley continues to serve as a member of the USA Women’s National Team Committee.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsty_Coventry
Title: Kirsty Coventry
Chunks: 6,7,8,9
At the 2005 World Championships in Montreal, Canada, Coventry improved on her 2004 Olympic medal count by winning gold in both the 100 m and 200 m backstroke and silver in the 200 m and the 400 m IM. She bettered her Olympic gold-winning 200 m backstroke time with a performance of 2:08.52. She was one of just two swimmers from Zimbabwe along with Warren Paynter.[28]
In Melbourne, Australia, at the 2007 World Championships, Coventry won silver medals in the 200 m backstroke and 200 m IM. She was disqualified in the 400 m IM when finishing second to eventual winner Katie Hoff in her heat. Coventry finished in a disappointing 14th place in the 100 m backstroke in a time of 1:01.73, failing to qualify for the final. She continued her good form of 2007 by winning four gold medals at the International Swim Meet in Narashino, Japan. She led the way in the 200 m and 400 m IM as well as the 100 m and 200 m backstroke.[29] In the 2007 All-Africa Games in Algiers, Algeria, Coventry won seven gold and three silver medals.[30]
2008 and 2009 seasonsedit  
Coventry in 2009
In 2008, Coventry broke her first world record in the 200 m backstroke at the Missouri Grand Prix. She bettered the mark set by Krisztina Egerszegi in August 1991, the second-oldest swimming world record. Her new record was 2:06.39. Coventry continued her winning streak at the meet by winning the 100 m backstroke and the 200 m IM. Coventry is the third woman in history to break the 1:00 minute barrier in the 100 m backstroke, and the second to break the 59-second barrier.[31]

At the 2008 Manchester Short Course World Championships, Coventry broke her second world record, setting a time, whilst winning the gold medal, of 4:26.52 in the 400 m IM. The following day saw Coventry win her second gold medal of the championships in the 100 m backstroke. Her time of 57:10 was a new championship record and the second-fastest time in history in the event. Only Natalie Coughlin has swum faster (56:51). Day three of the championships saw Coventry break another championship record in qualifying fastest for the final of the 200 m backstroke. Her time of 2:03.69 was a mere four-tenths of a second outside the current world record set by Reiko Nakamura in Tokyo in 2008. Coventry then bettered this time to take her second world record of the championships by winning the final in a time of 2:00.91. She then went on to shatter the short course World Record in winning the 200 m individual medley in 2:06.13.[32]

Coventry represented Zimbabwe at the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, China.[33] Coventry won the silver medal in the 400 metre individual medley event on 10 August 2008, becoming the second woman to swim the medley in less than 4:30, the first being Stephanie Rice who won the gold in the same event. Coventry beat the world record by just under two seconds and was only just beaten by Rice to a new world record. Coventry, in the second semi-final of the 100 m backstroke event, set a new world record of 58.77 seconds. In the final of that event, she was beaten to the gold medal by Natalie Coughlin. Coventry was again beaten by Stephanie Rice in the 200 m individual medley, despite swimming under the former world record. Coventry did defend her Olympic title in the 200 m backstroke, winning gold in a world record time of 2:05.24. She was the country's flag bearer at the closing ceremony. She was the lone member of the delegation to medal, helping win Zimbabwe's most medals at the Olympics ever.[34][35]
Awarded US$100,000 by President Mugabe for her success at the Olympics, Coventry gave that money to charity.[36] At the 2009 World Aquatics Championships in Rome, Italy, Coventry won a gold and a silver. She won the 200 m backstroke world title with a world record time and came second in the 400 m individual medley. She came fourth in the 200 m individual medley final and eighth in the 100 m backstroke final.[37]
2012 and 2016 Olympicsedit

Coventry qualified for her fourth Olympic Games in the 2012 Olympics in London, England. For the first time since 2000, Coventry did not win a medal. She finished third in her semifinal heat of the 200 m individual medley, just edging her into the final, where she placed 6th with a time of 2:11.13. In the 200 m backstroke, she finished outside medal contention in sixth place with a time of 2:08.18. She was given the honor of carrying the Zimbabwean flag into the opening ceremony for the first time.[38] Previously, Coventry won four gold and four silver medals in the 2011 All-Africa Games in Maputo, Mozambique.[39]
Her fifth and final Olympic appearance came at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil,[40] where she repeated her 6th-place performance in the 200 metre backstroke from 2012, with a time of 2:08.80. She also finished 11th in the 100 metre backstroke. She retired after the 2016 Olympics, where she carried the Zimbabwean flag into the stadium during the opening ceremony for the second and final time.[41][42] In her final African Games in 2015, in Brazzaville, the Republic of the Congo, Coventry won three golds and one bronze medals.[43]
Zimbabwean cabinetedit
On 7 September 2018, Coventry was appointed Minister of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation in Zimbabwe's cabinet under Zimbabwean president Emmerson Mnangagwa.[44] Her cabinet role led to her being dubbed "the soft face of Zimbabwe’s dictatorship" as she played a key role in the authoritarian regime.[10][9]

Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and current President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC). She won Olympic gold medals in the 2004 and 2008 Summer Games in women's swimming. She is an NCAA champion swimmer. She is currently presiding over the XXV Winter Olympic Games, the first games under her leadership. She is 42 years old (September 16, 1983) and was born in Harare, Zimbabwe, the country's capital and largest city.
Coventry was taught to swim by her mother when he was just a toddler in the family pool. She was inspired to compete at the Olympic level when she was watching the 1992 Games in Barcelona on television. She was a multi-sport athlete as a kid, competing in tennis, field hockey, and cross-country running. She focused on swimming after a knee injury as a young teen.

# Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and... - Living Legend Bios | Facebook
## Living Legend Bios's Post
Coventry competed in four events in the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, representing Zimbabwe. Her best finish was 12th in the 100m backstroke. After the Olympics, she moved to the United States and attended Auburn University on a scholarship. The Tigers dominated in swimming in the early 21st century with stars like Margaret Hoelzer, Eileen Coparropa, Maggie Bowen, and Coventry. The Tigers won three consecutive team NCAA championships (2002-04) while she was there under coach David Marsh. They were runner-up during her senior year in 2005. She won seven individual titles in her four years at Auburn. She earned a degree in Hotel and Restaurant Management.
In the middle of her collegiate career, Coventry made a return visit to the Olympics, this time to the 2004 Games in Athens. She won three medals, including a gold in the 200m backstroke. They were the only medals won by athletes from Zimbabwe. She wasn't done. She shattered the old world record by nearly a full second to defend her gold medal in the 2008 Games in Beijing. She set a world record in the semifinals of the 100m backstroke but was edged out for the gold by American Natalie Coughlin in the finals by about a quarter second. Coventry won two other silver medals at the games. She served as flag bearer for Zimbabwe in the closing ceremony.
Coventry returned to the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Games in London. This time, she was the flag bearer for the African country in the opening ceremony. She was hampered by pneumonia and injuring and her best finish was sixth. She was 32 years old when she last competed in the 2016 Summer Games in Rio de Janeiro, where she once again carried the Zimbabwean flag. Again, her best finish was sixth. She retired from competitive swimming after the 2016 Games.

# Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and... - Living Legend Bios | Facebook
## Living Legend Bios's Post
In 2012, Coventry was elected to the IOC Athletes' Commission. As a representative of that commission, she was elected as an IOC Member in 2013. She started on the IOC Executive Board in 2018. She was also appointed Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture in her home country by Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa in 2018. In 2025, she was elected as the 10th President of the IOC, succeeding German Thomas Bach, who served for nearly 12 years. On Friday (February 6th), she delivered a riveting speech in Milan, Italy, when the XXV Winter Olympic Games were declared open. The Games are expected to conclude on February 22. Her initial term ends in 2033.
Coventry and her husband founded The Kirsty Coventry Academy in 2015 to help address the high rate of drowning in her home country. It helps teach children from disadvantaged backgrounds swimming skills. They launched a program called HEROES (Health, Education, Recreation, Opportunity, Empowerment, Sport) in 2017 and provides free access to multi-sports for the children of Zimbabwe.
Coventry (pictured left in 2026) has two daughters (Ella pictured right in 2019) with Tyrone Seward. They have been married for 12 years. They primarily live in Lausanne, Switzerland.

## Living Legend Bios's Post
[February 8](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid02mE1gqUuNXyKst8hLKRnK8fjW7S4gZ7mjeRvCELDXYtbVkfPF4bsSmLMJkRtVXQmFl&id=100064131730429&__cft__[0]=AZiaKB_m-dwpkNW678iEBnvXyOdgWUfPK4UK8UyNy9HZE7a0XLHMtbdWOzXuotM3H7iaiQiXWx7cJGEQSvr2FWriD1KSikmCImhhVOQFB3mxkRlC1P6e6vOWsU8_8ySjjyjq_jyx7zS7MNRcMrEMpsM7VjFYh9yb&__tn__=%2CO%2CP-R) ·
Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and current President of the International Olympic Committee (IOC). She won Olympic gold medals in the 2004 and 2008 Summer Games in women's swimming. She is an NCAA champion swimmer. She is currently presiding over the XXV Winter Olympic Games, the first games under her leadership. She is 42 years old (September 16, 1983) and was born in Harare, Zimbabwe, the country's capital and largest city.
Coventry was taught to swim by her mother when he was just a toddler in the family pool. She was inspired to compete at the Olympic level when she was watching the 1992 Games in Barcelona on television. She was a multi-sport athlete as a kid, competing in tennis, field hockey, and cross-country running. She focused on swimming after a knee injury as a young teen.
texts.3:
# Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and... - Living Legend Bios | Facebook
## Living Legend Bios's Post
Coventry competed in four events in the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, representing Zimbabwe. Her best finish was 12th in the 100m backstroke. After the Olympics, she moved to the United States and attended Auburn University on a scholarship. The Tigers dominated in swimming in the early 21st century with stars like Margaret Hoelzer, Eileen Coparropa, Maggie Bowen, and Coventry. The Tigers won three consecutive team NCAA championships (2002-04) while she was there under coach David Marsh. They were runner-up during her senior year in 2005. She won seven individual titles in her four years at Auburn. She earned a degree in Hotel and Restaurant Management.
In the middle of her collegiate career, Coventry made a return visit to the Olympics, this time to the 2004 Games in Athens. She won three medals, including a gold in the 200m backstroke. They were the only medals won by athletes from Zimbabwe. She wasn't done. She shattered the old world record by nearly a full second to defend her gold medal in the 2008 Games in Beijing. She set a world record in the semifinals of the 100m backstroke but was edged out for the gold by American Natalie Coughlin in the finals by about a quarter second. Coventry won two other silver medals at the games. She served as flag bearer for Zimbabwe in the closing ceremony.
Coventry returned to the Olympics during the 2012 Summer Games in London. This time, she was the flag bearer for the African country in the opening ceremony. She was hampered by pneumonia and injuring and her best finish was sixth. She was 32 years old when she last competed in the 2016 Summer Games in Rio de Janeiro, where she once again carried the Zimbabwean flag. Again, her best finish was sixth. She retired from competitive swimming after the 2016 Games.
texts.4:
# Kirsty Leigh Coventry is the 10th and... - Living Legend Bios | Facebook
## Living Legend Bios's Post
In 2012, Coventry was elected to the IOC Athletes' Commission. As a representative of that commission, she was elected as an IOC Member in 2013. She started on the IOC Executive Board in 2018. She was also appointed Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture in her home country by Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa in 2018. In 2025, she was elected as the 10th President of the IOC, succeeding German Thomas Bach, who served for nearly 12 years. On Friday (February 6th), she delivered a riveting speech in Milan, Italy, when the XXV Winter Olympic Games were declared open. The Games are expected to conclude on February 22. Her initial term ends in 2033.
Coventry and her husband founded The Kirsty Coventry Academy in 2015 to help address the high rate of drowning in her home country. It helps teach children from disadvantaged backgrounds swimming skills. They launched a program called HEROES (Health, Education, Recreation, Opportunity, Empowerment, Sport) in 2017 and provides free access to multi-sports for the children of Zimbabwe.
Coventry (pictured left in 2026) has two daughters (Ella pictured right in 2019) with Tyrone Seward. They have been married for 12 years. They primarily live in Lausanne, Switzerland.

texts.6:
At the 2005 World Championships in Montreal, Canada, Coventry improved on her 2004 Olympic medal count by winning gold in both the 100 m and 200 m backstroke and silver in the 200 m and the 400 m IM. She bettered her Olympic gold-winning 200 m backstroke time with a performance of 2:08.52. She was one of just two swimmers from Zimbabwe along with Warren Paynter.[28]
In Melbourne, Australia, at the 2007 World Championships, Coventry won silver medals in the 200 m backstroke and 200 m IM. She was disqualified in the 400 m IM when finishing second to eventual winner Katie Hoff in her heat. Coventry finished in a disappointing 14th place in the 100 m backstroke in a time of 1:01.73, failing to qualify for the final. She continued her good form of 2007 by winning four gold medals at the International Swim Meet in Narashino, Japan. She led the way in the 200 m and 400 m IM as well as the 100 m and 200 m backstroke.[29] In the 2007 All-Africa Games in Algiers, Algeria, Coventry won seven gold and three silver medals.[30]
2008 and 2009 seasonsedit  
Coventry in 2009
In 2008, Coventry broke her first world record in the 200 m backstroke at the Missouri Grand Prix. She bettered the mark set by Krisztina Egerszegi in August 1991, the second-oldest swimming world record. Her new record was 2:06.39. Coventry continued her winning streak at the meet by winning the 100 m backstroke and the 200 m IM. Coventry is the third woman in history to break the 1:00 minute barrier in the 100 m backstroke, and the second to break the 59-second barrier.[31]
texts.7: At the 2008 Manchester Short Course World Championships, Coventry broke her second world record, setting a time, whilst winning the gold medal, of 4:26.52 in the 400 m IM. The following day saw Coventry win her second gold medal of the championships in the 100 m backstroke. Her time of 57:10 was a new championship record and the second-fastest time in history in the event. Only Natalie Coughlin has swum faster (56:51). Day three of the championships saw Coventry break another championship record in qualifying fastest for the final of the 200 m backstroke. Her time of 2:03.69 was a mere four-tenths of a second outside the current world record set by Reiko Nakamura in Tokyo in 2008. Coventry then bettered this time to take her second world record of the championships by winning the final in a time of 2:00.91. She then went on to shatter the short course World Record in winning the 200 m individual medley in 2:06.13.[32]
texts.8:
Coventry represented Zimbabwe at the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, China.[33] Coventry won the silver medal in the 400 metre individual medley event on 10 August 2008, becoming the second woman to swim the medley in less than 4:30, the first being Stephanie Rice who won the gold in the same event. Coventry beat the world record by just under two seconds and was only just beaten by Rice to a new world record. Coventry, in the second semi-final of the 100 m backstroke event, set a new world record of 58.77 seconds. In the final of that event, she was beaten to the gold medal by Natalie Coughlin. Coventry was again beaten by Stephanie Rice in the 200 m individual medley, despite swimming under the former world record. Coventry did defend her Olympic title in the 200 m backstroke, winning gold in a world record time of 2:05.24. She was the country's flag bearer at the closing ceremony. She was the lone member of the delegation to medal, helping win Zimbabwe's most medals at the Olympics ever.[34][35]
Awarded US$100,000 by President Mugabe for her success at the Olympics, Coventry gave that money to charity.[36] At the 2009 World Aquatics Championships in Rome, Italy, Coventry won a gold and a silver. She won the 200 m backstroke world title with a world record time and came second in the 400 m individual medley. She came fourth in the 200 m individual medley final and eighth in the 100 m backstroke final.[37]
2012 and 2016 Olympicsedit
texts.9:
Coventry qualified for her fourth Olympic Games in the 2012 Olympics in London, England. For the first time since 2000, Coventry did not win a medal. She finished third in her semifinal heat of the 200 m individual medley, just edging her into the final, where she placed 6th with a time of 2:11.13. In the 200 m backstroke, she finished outside medal contention in sixth place with a time of 2:08.18. She was given the honor of carrying the Zimbabwean flag into the opening ceremony for the first time.[38] Previously, Coventry won four gold and four silver medals in the 2011 All-Africa Games in Maputo, Mozambique.[39]
Her fifth and final Olympic appearance came at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil,[40] where she repeated her 6th-place performance in the 200 metre backstroke from 2012, with a time of 2:08.80. She also finished 11th in the 100 metre backstroke. She retired after the 2016 Olympics, where she carried the Zimbabwean flag into the stadium during the opening ceremony for the second and final time.[41][42] In her final African Games in 2015, in Brazzaville, the Republic of the Congo, Coventry won three golds and one bronze medals.[43]
Zimbabwean cabinetedit
On 7 September 2018, Coventry was appointed Minister of Youth, Sport, Arts and Recreation in Zimbabwe's cabinet under Zimbabwean president Emmerson Mnangagwa.[44] Her cabinet role led to her being dubbed "the soft face of Zimbabwe’s dictatorship" as she played a key role in the authoritarian regime.[10][9]
